title: What Does the Bible Say About Sex and the Body?
subtitle: What faithfulness asks of us on sex and the body in a culture that has rethought all of it.
question: When the culture has remade everything it once believed about sex, gender, and the body, and the church has answered with either surrender or cruelty, what does faithfulness actually look like? Not a slogan. Not a rally. A way of living in a body that the world calls infinitely changeable and the church too often calls a problem to be managed.
whyItMatters:
This is the wound nobody escapes. Every person carries a body, and almost every person carries some grief about it, some failure, some longing the church never knew how to name without flinching. The sexual revolution did not arrive as a theory. It arrived as a thousand quiet decisions about what a body is for, and the church met it badly from both directions, dissolving its teaching into the culture on one side and weaponizing that teaching into shame on the other.

I am not writing from a safe distance. I have sat with the woman who was taught she was damaged goods at sixteen and never recovered. I have sat with the gay teenager whose parents loved Jesus and could not look at him. I have watched the church thunder about other people's beds while ignoring the lust, the divorce, the abuse inside its own walls. If we cannot hold the truth and the tenderness at the same time, we have no business speaking at all.
biblicalFoundation:
Begin where Scripture begins, with a body called good. Genesis does not treat flesh as the prison of a pure soul. God forms the man from dust and calls the whole arrangement very good. The body is not the obstacle to holiness. It is the site of it. Whatever the church later absorbed from Greek suspicion of the flesh, the Hebrew Scriptures never wavered. The body is a gift, not a shame.

Then the claim deepens past anything the ancient world expected. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. God did not redeem us from bodies. He took one on. And he did not leave it in the grave. The resurrection is the final word on whether matter matters, whether these aching, desiring, mortal bodies are worth anything to God. They are worth a cross and an empty tomb. Christopher West built a whole theology of the body on this refusal to treat flesh as cheap, and he was reading Paul rightly.

Inside this dignity, Scripture sets sex within covenant. The one-flesh union of Genesis is not a rule bolted onto desire. It is a sign. Paul says the marriage of a man and a woman points past itself to Christ and the church, the whole story of a God who binds himself to a people and will not let them go. Sex carries that weight precisely because the body is good and the covenant is real. To sever it from covenant is not to free it. It is to empty it of the thing that made it mean so much.

And so the call to chastity, which the modern ear hears as repression and Scripture means as integrity, the body and the promises aligned. Chastity is not a single-people problem. It is the married person's faithfulness and the single person's faithfulness, the same virtue in two settings. Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, Paul tells the Corinthians, not to shame them but to dignify them, you were bought at a price. Every person reading this was made in the image of God, is loved past comprehension, and is invited into a holiness that honors the flesh rather than despising it. Wesley Hill has lived this as a celibate gay Christian, and his witness is that the historic ethic, held with honesty, is a hard grace and not a cruelty.
keyTexts: Genesis 1:27 to 31, humanity made male and female in God's image, and the whole creation called very good
Genesis 2:24, the one-flesh union, the first covenant of the body
John 1:14, the Word became flesh, the incarnation that forever dignifies the body
1 Corinthians 6:12 to 20, the body as a temple of the Holy Spirit, bought at a price
Ephesians 5:25 to 32, marriage as a sign pointing to Christ and the church
Romans 8:11 to 23, the redemption of the body and the resurrection hope

churchRecord.led: In the first centuries the church held a sexual ethic so strange it remade the ancient world. Rome assumed a free man could use slaves, children, and prostitutes as he pleased, and that infants could be exposed on hillsides to die. The early Christians refused all of it. They rescued the abandoned babies, many of them girls left to die. They told the powerful man that his body and the slave's body answered to the same God. They lifted up women and the vulnerable by insisting that no one was disposable and no body was a thing to be used. This ethic protected the weak from the strong, and that is exactly why it spread.
churchRecord.failed: And then, across long stretches of its history, the church betrayed its own gift. Purity culture taught a generation that a girl who had been touched was a chewed piece of gum, and it has spent decades sitting with the wreckage. It turned the gospel of a Savior who ate with sinners into a single obsession with whose body did what, while greed and pride and cruelty walked the aisles unrebuked. It treated gay people with a contempt that has no warrant anywhere in the teaching of Jesus, driving children out of homes and into despair. Worst of all, it covered abuse, again and again, protecting institutions and predators while the wounded were told to forgive and be quiet. The church that once shielded the vulnerable learned, in too many places, to shield the powerful instead.

whereWeAgree: Start with what almost everyone who fears God can still say together. Every single person bears the image of God, the gay teenager and the divorced deacon and the woman the church wrote off, every one of them carries the weight of glory and is loved without condition by the One who made them. And the body matters. It is not a costume or a cage. It is good, it is dignified by the incarnation, and what we do with it and to it is never trivial. These two things, the worth of the person and the goodness of the body, are common ground we abandoned far too easily.
captureLeft: On one side the church surrenders. To be accepted, to stop being the embarrassing relative at the cultural table, it quietly lets its historic teaching dissolve into whatever the moment affirms. It treats the body as infinitely changeable, raw material for the will, and calls this liberation. It reduces a person to the sum of their desires and then calls any desire sacred. It follows the culture wherever the culture goes and names the following courage. This is not love. It is the abandonment of a costly inheritance dressed up as compassion, and the people it claims to serve are left with a church that believes nothing it can lean on.
captureRight: On the other side the church hardens into idol. Purity culture became a religion of its own, where a body's worth was measured by what had or had not happened to it, and the cross dropped out entirely. The church aimed a cruelty at gay people that it never aimed at the gluttonous or the greedy, singling out one sin as the unforgivable one while its own divorce rate matched the world's. It handed its sexual ethic to a political movement to be waved like a flag, trading the prophetic for the partisan. And it thundered about everyone else's lust while burying its own, the pastor's affair, the elder's pornography, the abuse in the youth wing. It condemned the bodies of strangers and protected the appetites of insiders.
whereWeDiffer: Now name the division plainly, because pretending it does not exist helps no one. Faithful Christians who love Jesus and trust the Scriptures divide, deeply and sincerely, between the historic or traditional view, that sex belongs within the covenant of a man and a woman, and the affirming view, that committed same-sex unions can be blessed. This is not a gap between believers and unbelievers. It runs straight through the church, through families, through denominations, between people who pray to the same Lord. I hold the historic view, and I will not pretend the disagreement is small or that the people on the other side of it are my enemies. And even within the historic view, pastoral approaches differ sharply, between those who lead with the law and those who lead with the long, patient nearness of Christ. Honesty about all of this is the beginning of any conversation worth having.
theCost: To hold a countercultural ethic with real compassion is to be trusted by neither side. The culture will call you a bigot for believing anything ancient about the body. The hardliners in your own church will call you a compromiser for refusing to be cruel. You will be too soft for the rally and too firm for the parade. The cost is to live in that exposed middle without flinching toward either escape, refusing cowardice, which dissolves the truth to be liked, and refusing cruelty, which wields the truth to wound. It is far easier to pick a tribe and let it tell you whom to despise. Faithfulness will not let you.
charge: So here is the weight I cannot set down. I have been both kinds of unfaithful. I have softened the hard word to keep a room comfortable, and I have wielded the hard word to make myself feel clean. I have stood at a distance from the people most wounded by the church's failures and called my distance conviction. The body declared good in the garden, dignified at Bethlehem, raised on Easter, is the same body I have used to judge and the same body God will not give up on. We did this, the surrender and the cruelty both, and we did it to people Christ died for. The question is not whether the culture has gone wrong. The question is whether the church will become a place where a broken body can come home without being lied to or stoned. I do not yet know if we have the courage. That is what remains.

right.label: The Right Capture
right.whatItLooksLike: The historic ethic hardens into an idol of purity and a weapon of the culture war. The body's worth is measured by what has happened to it, one sin is singled out as unforgivable, and the church's own lust and divorce and abuse go unnamed while it condemns the bodies of strangers.
right.inThePast: For decades a whole industry of purity rallies, virginity pledges, and courtship manuals taught young people, girls most of all, that their value rose and fell with their sexual history. Shame was the engine, and the gospel of grace went missing. Alongside it ran movements promising to change a person's orientation, leaving deep harm in their wake.
right.now: The same instinct survives by attaching the church's sexual ethic to partisan politics, treating the bodies of gay and trans people as a battlefield for electoral advantage rather than as people to be loved. The cruelty is now defended as bravery, and the hypocrisy of condemning outsiders while shielding insiders has only grown more brazen.

left.label: The Left Capture
left.whatItLooksLike: The church abandons its historic teaching to be accepted by the culture, treating the body as infinitely changeable and the self as nothing more than the sum of its desires. The costly inheritance dissolves quietly into whatever the moment affirms, and the surrender is renamed compassion.
left.inThePast: The wider sexual revolution recast sex as recreation severed from covenant and consequence, and large parts of the church, rather than offering a wiser word, simply absorbed the new assumptions a half-step behind the culture, embarrassed by anything that sounded ancient.
left.now: Whole denominations have revised their historic teaching to align with the surrounding consensus, and a popular theology reduces personal identity to felt desire while treating the body as raw material for the will. The historic ethic is quietly retired as an embarrassment, and the people it once steadied are left with a church that asks nothing and so can promise nothing.
named: the mainline denominational shifts to fully affirming positions
the wider sexual revolution and its severing of sex from covenant
the reduction of personal identity to the sum of one's desires

the deconstruction movement that discards the historic ethic as mere oppression
the therapeutic gospel that asks nothing of the body and so steadies no one
